findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit the cancellable request context
findings.body: Create derives the legacy goroutine's context from the incoming request context, and the same pattern is used by Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection. The API server can cancel that context as soon as Create returns the unified-storage response, which happens immediately after spawning the goroutine, so the legacy write will often run with an already-cancelled context and fail. This defeats the stated safety purpose of mode 3. The legacy context needs to be detached from request cancellation, for example with context.WithoutCancel plus its own timeout, while preserving needed values.

findings.title: Unordered legacy goroutines can resurrect or lose objects
findings.body: Every Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection launches an independent legacy goroutine with no per-resource ordering or queue. Rapid operations on the same object can therefore reach legacy storage out of order: a delete can run before the preceding create and leave a resurrected object, or an update can run before its create and be lost. The previous synchronous implementation preserved request order, so legacy storage can now silently diverge from unified storage.

findings.title: Create shares the same object between the response and legacy goroutine
findings.body: Create passes the original obj pointer to the asynchronous Legacy.Create while returning the unified-storage result to the caller. The storage implementation may have mutated obj, and the caller/API server may concurrently serialize or mutate the returned object while the goroutine reads the same underlying object, creating a data race. The legacy call can also observe storage-assigned fields such as resourceVersion that a legacy create does not expect. Legacy needs its own deep copy made before the goroutine is started.

findings.title: Update recomputes the updated object separately for legacy storage
findings.body: Update now passes the original objInfo to Legacy.Update after Storage.Update has already consumed it. Each storage will invoke UpdatedObject against its own old object, so transformations, defaults, timestamps, or other computed fields can differ between unified and legacy storage, and a stateful UpdatedObject implementation may fail or behave differently on the second call. The removed updateWrapper existed to compute the object once and give both stores the identical result; that guarantee needs to be restored for the legacy write.

findings.title: Delete no longer cleans up legacy objects when unified delete reports NotFound
findings.body: Delete now returns immediately for any Storage.Delete error. The previous implementation specifically tolerated NotFound and still attempted the legacy delete. An object that exists only in legacy storage, or whose unified copy was already removed, will now remain in legacy storage and can reappear if traffic is rolled back to a legacy-reading mode. NotFound from unified storage should still trigger the legacy deletion attempt.

findings.title: Several dual-writer metrics are recorded against the wrong storage or label
findings.body: When Storage.Create fails, Create calls recordLegacyDuration instead of recording a storage failure, and Update does the same at its storage-error path. DeleteCollection records the asynchronous legacy result with recordStorageDuration, while Delete's success path passes the resource name where other calls pass options.Kind as the kind label. This corrupts the mode-3 dashboards/error attribution and, for Delete, introduces a high-cardinality metric label containing object names.

findings.title: Asynchronous legacy failures are silently swallowed
findings.body: The legacy goroutines in Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection capture the legacy error only to update a duration metric and never log it. The previous synchronous implementation logged legacy write failures. Operators therefore get no object identity or error context when legacy storage starts diverging, making the safety copy unreliable and difficult to diagnose or reconcile.

findings.title: Mode 3 tests never synchronize with or verify the async legacy writes
findings.body: The new Create and Update tests register legacy mock expectations but return immediately after asserting only the unified-storage result; Delete and DeleteCollection do not meaningfully verify a legacy call at all. Nothing waits for the goroutines, calls AssertExpectations, or uses.Eventually, so a legacy write that never happens can still pass, while a goroutine running after the test finishes can produce racy or unexpected mock calls. The async behavior that defines mode 3 is therefore untested.

findings.title: New mode 3 integration cases immediately assert legacy visibility despite async writes
findings.body: The added file and unified-storage mode 3 cases reuse doPlaylistTests, which creates, updates, and deletes through the Kubernetes API and then immediately checks the legacy playlist API for the same state. Mode 3 performs legacy writes in fire-and-forget goroutines with no completion signal, so those legacy assertions race the asynchronous writes and will be flaky even if they usually win the race in local runs.
